first.rationale: The two observed declines (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) point at the funnel itself, not at price, so the highest-leverage single slot is onboarding simplification (memory_86, reinforced by memory_31). I spend the one verification pull on memory_86 rather than on a memory I do not intend to act on, because memory_86 is both the load-bearing basis for the action and the one most likely to be over-read: as summarized it reports completion rate and time-to-value, which are proxy metrics, and says nothing about whether the lift persisted into qualified revenue or retention. The archived record should tell me whether the original experiment measured downstream conversion and account quality, or only funnel throughput. That distinction matters because the failure mode here is real: stripping required fields and steps can inflate activation counts while degrading lead qualification, routing, and eventual paid conversion, which would hurt the primary objective even as the dashboard improves. I deliberately did not choose promotional_pricing (memory_73) despite the competitor's entry pricing; discount-led response to a price attack is the classic way to buy unqualified, low-retention volume and compress margin, and memory_73's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is exactly the kind of claim whose durability is unverified. Referral incentives (memory_57) target existing customers and do not address the observed funnel decline; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is plausible but addresses a different segment than the one that is bleeding. I will run this as a standard experiment with a holdout, and I will hold the readout on downstream qualified revenue and week-four retention, not on completion rate alone. If verification shows memory_86 only ever measured completion, I will treat the expected effect as unproven on the metric that actually matters and shrink to a guarded test with quality gates rather than proceeding at full scale.

final.rationale:
Verification strengthened the case but did not fully close it. exp_86 reports completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — that last figure is the one I was worried about, and it argues the completion lift was not hollow throughput. A shortened flow that also improves 30-day retention is unlikely to be pure funnel inflation. That said, 30-day retention is still not qualified revenue; the record does not show paid conversion, deal size, or lead-routing quality, so the link from this intervention to the primary objective remains inferred rather than demonstrated. I am proceeding, not treating the question as settled.

Simplify_onboarding remains the best use of the single slot because it is the only direction aimed squarely at the two metrics actually declining (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and it is now the best-evidenced direction in the inherited set. Activation_messaging (memory_91) targets the same funnel but is the weaker, less-verified sibling and would be my fallback. I continue to decline promotional_pricing (memory_73) despite the competitor's entry pricing: matching a price attack with discounts buys volume that is selected for price sensitivity and tends to churn, which is the direct opposite of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and memory_73's durability was never checked. Referral_incentive (memory_57) does not touch the failing funnel; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) serves a segment that is not the one bleeding.

Standard experiment with a holdout. I will read out on downstream qualified revenue and paid conversion as primary, with completion rate as a secondary diagnostic only, and I will monitor lead-quality and routing fields I remove so I can tell whether any activation gain is being paid for with worse qualification. If qualified revenue is flat or negative while completion rises, I stop and revert rather than declaring success on the proxy — that is the specific failure mode this action carries, and verification reduced but did not eliminate it.
